request.task: What exactly does `git reset --hard HEAD~1` do to the last commit and to any uncommitted changes in the working tree? Be precise and brief.

final.final_answer:
`git reset --hard HEAD~1` moves the current branch pointer (and `HEAD`) back one commit, to the parent of the current commit, and then forces both the index (staging area) and the working tree to exactly match that parent commit.

Effect on the last commit: it is removed from the branch's history — it's no longer reachable from the branch tip — but it is typically recoverable for a period of time via `git reflog` (as long as garbage collection hasn't run). Reflog entries are commonly retained for at least 30 days, and at least 90 days if the commit is an ancestor of the branch tip, though eventually `git gc` can clean them up permanently.

Effect on uncommitted changes: any staged and unstaged modifications to tracked files are discarded and overwritten to match the parent commit. Untracked files are left untouched — Git's reset does not delete them; a separate command (`git clean`) is required to remove untracked files.
final.label: verified
caveats: Position(s) s2 were set aside because cited sources settled an axis against them; they could not then win on a head-count.

Surviving dissent (s2): one position holds that the reset 'permanently discards the commit and all uncommitted changes.' This was not adopted — evidence (reflog behavior documented via Stack Overflow and GitHub's own blog, and Git's handling of untracked files) shows the commit is generally recoverable via `git reflog` for a window of time, and untracked files are never touched by `--hard` reset.

This would change if: recovery via reflog is not truly available in your situation — e.g., if `git gc` has already run and pruned unreachable commits, or enough time (30–90+ days) has passed for reflog entries to expire, making the commit unrecoverable in practice.

Read as a reset of tracked changes and history reachability only — if you meant whether untracked files might also be lost, the answer changes to: no, untracked files are unaffected by `--hard` reset and require a separate `git clean` to remove.

payload.justification: The answers disagree on two critical, factual points that affect user actions: 1) whether the discarded commit is permanently lost or recoverable via `git reflog`, which determines if a user tries to recover from a mistake, and 2) whether untracked files are deleted, which determines if a user needs to back them up before running the command. Answer A correctly states the commit is recoverable and untracked files are safe, while B and C incorrectly state the commit is permanently lost and omit any mention of untracked files.

payload.question: Is the commit removed by `git reset --hard` permanently lost or is it recoverable?
payload.decision_impact: If the commit is permanently lost, a user who runs the command by mistake will believe their work is gone and will not attempt to recover it. If the commit is recoverable via the reflog, the user can take steps to restore it.

positions.s1: The commit is not permanently lost and can typically be recovered using `git reflog`.
positions.s2: The commit is permanently lost or deleted.

payload.decision_impact: If untracked files are deleted by the command, a user must back them up before running it. If untracked files are not affected, this precaution is unnecessary.

positions.s1: No, untracked files are not removed.

[github.blog](https://github.blog/open-source/git/how-to-undo-almost-anything-with-git/) confirms: "git reflog is an amazing resource for recovering project history. payload.summary: Multiple sources confirm that `git reset --hard` does NOT affect untracked files. [git-scm.com](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-reset.html) documents that the command updates tracked files and the index, but [stackoverflow.com](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/36349351/git-reset-hard-doesnt-make-the-working-tree-look-like-index) explicitly states: "Remember that resetting only affects tracked files, so a separate command is required for cleaning up untracked ones" and "There is one important rule that Git will always follow (unless explicitly told not to do it): Do not touch untracked file." The same source explains that Git has a safety mechanism: "Using the default functionality, Git will never perform any action that will end up in a data loss of untracked files" because "information from untracked files can never be recovered by Git." To remove untracked files, a separate command (`git clean`) is required. Position s1 is correct; s2's implication that untracked files may be at risk is contradicted by the sources. | Multiple official Git documentation sources explicitly state that `git reset --hard` does NOT affect untracked files. [git-scm.com](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-reset.html) states the command "may overwrite untracked files" in the context of describing what happens to tracked files, but clarifies that untracked files are not removed. [stackoverflow.com](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/34149356/what-exactly-is-the-difference-between-all-the-git-reset-modes) provides a detailed comparison table showing "Untracked files" with dashes across all reset modes, explicitly noting "(Spoiler: No)" untracked files will be changed. The documentation consistently distinguishes between tracked and untracked files, with untracked files remaining untouched. Position s1 is correct: untracked files are not removed by `git reset --hard`. Position s2's implication that untracked files "may be at risk" is not supported by the sources.
